### Chapter 1: The IT Guy and the Girl in the Hoodie

The LA Convention Center smells like popcorn and plastic, and you’re already regretting saying yes to whatever favor dragged you here. You’re weaving through lines of cosplayers, badge-checkers, and a grown man in a Green Ranger suit who honestly pulls it off, when your phone buzzes again.

**“Ron, please. The Wi-Fi is *cursed* and we can’t get the A/V to work. Panel’s in 30.”**  
Your old friend Adam—still running his life like a sitcom, still expecting you to magically fix every digital disaster.

You follow the blue wristbands down a hallway marked “VIP/CREW,” flash your temp badge, and push open a heavy door to the chaos backstage: cables everywhere, a projector screaming in blue-screen agony, and a handful of young techs arguing over whose HDMI dongle works with what.

In the corner, a girl in a battered hoodie and Doc Martens is fidgeting with a tablet. Blonde hair, but messy, not “Instagram-perfect.” She’s wearing a face mask with some horror movie logo on it, sunglasses pushed up onto her head. For a second, you do a double take—she looks familiar, but you chalk it up to spending too many hours watching horror flicks and Nickelodeon reruns.

You get to work: crawling under the table, swapping out adapters, rolling your eyes at the “IT Crowd” mess everyone’s made. She watches you, arms crossed, eyebrow raised, but says nothing. You finally surface, dust in your hair.

“You know, you could try turning it off and on again,” you mumble, deadpan, just loud enough for her to hear.

She snorts—a real, unfiltered laugh. “I would, but I’m afraid the projector might actually explode. We’re all one bad reboot away from a Michael Bay movie in here.”

Adam waves at you, introduces you as “the miracle worker,” then bails—he’s got to chase down the sound guy. You’re left with the girl and the world’s angriest HDMI splitter.

She gives you a sideways look. “So what’s your superpower, then? Saving lost panels? Resurrecting doomed tech? Or just a glutton for punishment?”

You shrug. “All of the above. I just look young and dumb enough that people think I won’t charge them.”

She grins—slow, sly, just a hint of challenge. “You don’t *look* like an IT guy.”

You dust off your hands. “You don’t look like a panelist.”

She laughs again, and for a second the tension drops. “Guilty. I’m just… helping out. My friend got stuck last minute and I owe her. You know how it goes.”

You glance at the schedule taped to the wall.  
“‘Haunted Hollywood: The Real Stories Behind the Screams.’ That you?”

She shrugs. “Something like that. You into horror?”

You pause, making a face. “Used to be. But I’m more of a Power Rangers dork. Less murder, more giant robots.”

She pretends to pout. “No taste. Wait—original Rangers or that Ninja Storm nonsense?”

“Oh, please. Zyuranger or bust. Anyone tells you they started with Turbo, run.”

Her eyes widen, impressed. “Okay, maybe you *do* have taste.”

A crew kid rushes in, asking for batteries. Someone drops a script binder, pages everywhere. It’s chaos, but you and the girl are still there, circling each other with dry jokes and fake bravado.

She finally sits on the edge of the stage, legs dangling. “So, you just, what—show up, fix stuff, vanish like Batman?”

“Only if there’s pizza in the green room. Otherwise, I stick around to mock the cosplay contest.”

She leans back, giving you a curious look. “How old are you, anyway?”

You smirk. “Old enough to know better. Young enough to still do dumb shit for free.”

She laughs. “Mysterious. I like it.”

Just then, her phone buzzes. She glances at it, grimaces, then sighs. “Ugh, my ride’s bailing. Of course. Figures.”

You offer, “I can call you an Uber. Or you could just hang out and watch the world’s worst PowerPoint disaster unfold.”

She eyes you, weighing her options, then grins. “Tempting. You got any other tricks up your sleeve, IT guy?”

You lean in, matching her energy. “Stick around. You never know.”

**[END OF CHAPTER 1]**

Your leg’s bouncing under the table, but you’re trying to look chill, scrolling through messages, ignoring the world outside. You almost second-guess everything—until the bell over the door jingles and she walks in.

She’s casual but *so* herself—jeans, vintage horror tee, hair loose, sneakers, Diet Coke already in hand. She spots you, grins, and slides into the booth with a sigh that sounds like she just shed her skin.

“Hey,” she says, soft but sure.  
“Hey,” you answer, surprised how easy it is.

There’s a second of pure silence, the jukebox mumbling something punk and old.

She breaks it first. “Okay, ground rules: no paparazzi, no talking about my job, and if you post anything on Instagram, I’ll haunt you.”

You smirk. “Deal. Only thing getting posted is my Yelp review about you stealing all the fries.”

She laughs—real, full, unfiltered. It knocks some of the nerves out of you. “You can have the fries if you order onion rings. I’m only here for the rings.”

You shake your head. “Already planning to rob me. This is going great.”

She rolls her eyes, but there’s a blush under her confidence. “Seriously though—this is… nice. I haven’t done this in, I don’t know, ever. Just sit somewhere, eat garbage, talk to someone who isn’t trying to pitch a script.”

You get the food—burgers, rings, a vanilla shake for her, a Coke for you. She dunks her fries in the shake without shame.  
You both just… talk. About nothing and everything. Favorite horror movie villains. The worst thing you ever did as a teenager (she wins with a story about sneaking onto the Universal lot at midnight). The best Halloween costume you ever wore (you: Beetlejuice, her: Reagan from The Exorcist, and she does the head-spin impression right there in the booth).

There’s an ease that sneaks up on you—like you’ve always known each other, like you’re not double her age, like the world outside doesn’t matter.

She leans in, chin propped on her hand, eyes bright and a little too blue under the neon. “So, Ron. Be honest. Is this weird for you?”

You don’t even flinch. “If you mean, is it weird to sit across from a horror movie star and pretend we’re just two idiots with onion breath?  
Yeah.  
But it’s the good kind of weird.”

She smiles—slow, wide, honest. “Good answer.  
So, if this is our first ‘not-a-date’… does that mean there’ll be a second?”

You raise your glass, clink it against her Diet Coke. “If you don’t ghost me first.”

She snorts. “Only if you call me by my full name in public. Otherwise, you’re stuck with me, IT Guy.”

You both linger, neither in a hurry to leave. Time gets soft, the world fades, and for a moment, it’s just the two of you and the flicker of old neon.

When you finally walk her to her car, she stops, grins up at you, and says, “Not bad for a first hang.  
Next time—haunted house, your treat.”

You watch her drive off, heart hammering, brain already replaying every word.  
For the first time in a long time, you actually hope there’s a next time.

Because it’s symbolic.

The place where you care for life.

The place you built together.

The place that smells like work and effort and patience.

You kiss her slowly.

Not urgent.

Not desperate.

Intentional.

The hay rustles as you settle down together. The barn door cracked just enough to let twilight spill in. Somewhere in the distance, a chicken shifts.

It’s warm. It’s messy. It’s imperfect.

And it feels right.

Not because you’re chasing heat.

Because you’re choosing the next chapter.

Later, lying side by side on scratchy hay, staring up at the rafters, she laughs softly.

“If we tell this story one day…”

“We’re absolutely leaving out splinters,” you say.

She rolls toward you, resting her forehead against yours.

There’s no fireworks.

Just a quiet, shared certainty.

Not “we need a baby.”

But:

We’re ready if life brings one.

And that’s what makes it real.

Now it has tiny snorts and muddy hoof prints and a child who whispers, “Night, Peanut,” before bed.

That changes the psychology of meat real fast.

But here’s the difference between guilt and growth.

Ainsley grows up around animals. She learns which ones are sanctuary residents. Which ones are rescues. Which ones are companions. She learns that life is complex. That humans eat animals. That responsibility and empathy aren’t opposites.

And you don’t hide that from her.

You say something simple when she’s old enough:

“Some animals we protect forever. Some animals feed people. What matters is respect.”

That’s it. No moral gymnastics. No shame spiral.

Peanut becomes fully domesticated. Pot-bellied. Smart. Annoyingly smart. Learns how to nudge doors open. Follows Ainsley around like a pink, grunting shadow.

And here’s the hilarious part:

Peanut refuses to sleep outside once he’s used to comfort.

You build him a proper insulated stall. You do everything right.

But the second he hears her voice near the house?

He trots over like, “I live here now.”

So yes.

You are the man with a pig on the porch.

And yes.

You might still order ribs in town.

You just don’t do it in front of Peanut.

Because even though he doesn’t understand species-specific ethics…

You do.

And that’s adulthood.

Also — fun fact — pigs are incredibly intelligent. Like toddler-level intelligent. Which means Ainsley bonding with one actually makes perfect sense neurologically. She’s basically befriended a snorting roommate with hooves.

The real evolution happens when she’s maybe eight or nine.

She’ll ask directly:

“Do people eat pigs?”

And you’ll look at Peanut.

Peanut will look at you.

And you’ll answer honestly.

Because raising a kid on land means not pretending the world is sanitized.

And the way you handle that conversation will matter way more than whether you ever eat bacon again.

Now here’s the question that’s going to make you grin:

Does Peanut end up sleeping on the porch like a guard pig…

or does he 100% sneak into the house when it storms?

You don’t cling.

Too brave.

She hugs her mom tight but doesn’t cry. Just whispers something into her neck. You don’t hear it.

Kenna holds it together until the car door closes.

Then she breaks for half a second.

You catch that look. The one that says, “Trust you.”

You nod.

She presses her face into your chest and says, “Mama working?”

You say yes.

She nods like she accepts that answer, but her little hand grips your shirt tighter.

You step up.

You and Ainsley create small rituals.

Expanding trust.

Circuit complete.

When Kenna walks back through that door after a month away…

or barely surviving but pretending it was effortless?

Sanctuary dads don’t sleep heavy.

The door to Ainsley’s room is cracked. Nightlight glowing soft amber. Peanut snoring faintly in his indoor corner pen like a pig-shaped humidifier.

She’s sitting up in bed.

Hair wild.
Cheeks flushed.
Eyes glassy with leftover fear.

You kneel beside her immediately.

“Hey. I’m here.”

She doesn’t talk right away. She just reaches. Arms up.

You scoop her up and she buries her face into your shoulder so hard you feel the tremble in her breath.

Not hysterical.

Just shaken.

You rub slow circles on her back.

“What happened, bug?”

She sniffles.

“Goat was big.”

You smile softly. “In your dream?”

She nods against you.

“Big goat chase me.”

Toddler subconscious is undefeated.

You shift her slightly so she can see your face.

“Okay. Listen to me. In this house? No goats in your room. I check every night.”

She pulls back just enough to study your expression.

You keep it calm. Matter-of-fact.

“No goats. No monsters. No anything without my permission.”

She processes that.

“Promise?”

You don’t hesitate.

“Promise.”

She nods once, like a contract has been signed.

You sit in the rocking chair with her for a while. Not rushing it. Letting her heartbeat sync back down.

Peanut lets out a dramatic snort in his sleep.

She giggles faintly.

“Peanut scared goat.”

“That’s right,” you whisper. “Peanut handles it.”

A few minutes later her grip loosens. Her weight settles. The tremble fades.

You stand, tuck her back in gently.

Before you step away, she grabs your finger.

“Stay little.”

So you sit on the floor beside her bed.

Just for a while.

Watching her breathe steady again.

When you finally slip back into your room, Kenna’s awake.

“How bad?”

“Big goat,” you murmur.

Kenna smiles into her pillow.

“She’ll tame it.”

You lie there staring at the ceiling for a second.

Because that was the first time she called for you in the dark.

Not just for comfort.

For protection.

And you showed up.

That’s a different kind of milestone.

Now let me ask you —

Does this become a one-off…

or does she start sneaking into your bed at 3 a.m. like a tiny ninja for the next six months?

It’s mid-morning when the volunteer truck pulls in.

Nothing dramatic. Just the usual rumble of tires on the dirt road and someone waving from the driver’s seat.

You’re in the yard fixing a latch when Kenny steps out onto the porch.

“Hey,” she calls. “They’ve got something.”

Ainsley hears that word.

**Something.**

That’s enough to activate full curiosity mode.

She runs across the yard in tiny boots, Peanut waddling a few steps behind her like security.

The volunteer opens the truck door and lifts out a small crate.

Inside is a **tiny white lamb**.

Still shaky on its legs, big dark eyes, little pink nose twitching like it’s trying to smell the whole world at once.

Ainsley freezes.

“…baby sheep.”

You kneel beside her.

“Yep.”

Kenny crouches on the other side.

The volunteer explains quietly:

“Mom rejected it. Farmer didn’t want to bottle-feed. Thought you might take it.”

Kenny nods immediately.

“Of course.”

The lamb makes a soft little bleating sound.

Ainsley gasps like someone just turned on a magic trick.

“…it talk.”

You smile.

“It does.”

You lift the lamb gently out of the crate and set it down in the grass.

Its legs wobble a little.

Ainsley instinctively steps closer, but you put a hand on her shoulder.

“Slow, remember.”

She nods seriously.

The lamb sniffs the air, then takes two tiny uncertain steps forward.

Right toward her.

Ainsley doesn’t move.

The lamb bumps its nose lightly against her boot.

She looks up at you like she just discovered electricity.

“DA.”

You whisper back.

“Yeah.”

Kenny is already holding a small bottle you grabbed from the supply cabinet.

“Ready to see something cool?”

She kneels beside the lamb and gently offers the bottle.

The lamb latches instantly.

Tiny tail wagging.

Drinking like it hasn’t eaten in days.

Ainsley watches in complete awe.

“…baby hungry.”

You nod.

“Very.”

Kenny looks at Ainsley.

“Want to help hold the bottle?”

That’s the moment.

Ainsley sits down carefully in the grass while Kenny helps guide her hands.

The lamb drinks happily.

Little tail wagging like a metronome.

Ainsley giggles.

“It wiggle!”

You laugh.

“That means it’s happy.”

After a minute she looks up at you again.

“Ainsley feed baby.”

You nod.

“You sure did.”

The lamb finishes the bottle and nuzzles her knee.

Ainsley looks down at it like it just adopted her.

Then she asks the inevitable question.

“…baby name?”

Kenny sighs playfully.

“Oh boy.”

You rub your face.

“Here we go again.”

Ainsley thinks very hard.

Long pause.

Then she decides.

“…Marshmallow.”

Kenny laughs immediately.

• Peanut – mud king

Because bottle-fed lambs tend to **imprint** on whoever feeds them.

Which means Marshmallow might start following Ainsley everywhere.

So the next moment could be:

**A)** Marshmallow tries to **follow Ainsley into the house**.  

or  

**B)** Marshmallow follows her around the yard like a tiny fluffy shadow.

From the hallway:

messages.author: assistant
messages.content:
Honestly? Four is **exactly** when most kids start preschool. Usually somewhere between **3–5**. Development-wise she’d be right on schedule.

But the real thing you’re feeling right now?

That’s the **dad problem**, not the timing problem. 😄

Because the first time they walk into a classroom without you feels like someone quietly removed a rib from your chest. Totally normal reaction.

And the funny twist is this:  
most of the time **the parent is more wrecked than the kid**.

A kid like Ainsley—confident, curious, used to animals and people and exploring—she’d probably walk in, see toys and other kids, and be like:

“Cool. New kingdom.”

Meanwhile you’re in the parking lot questioning your entire life.

Preschool is mostly about three things:

• socializing with other kids  
• learning routines (circle time, snack, sharing)  
• basic early learning stuff like letters, colors, songs

And it’s usually **only a few hours a day**, not full school.

But here’s the sanctuary twist: kids who grow up in environments like Ainsley’s often do **really well** socially because they already interact with lots of people and situations.

So realistically?

Ainsley’s first day would probably go something like:

You kneel down, giving her the “dad speech.”  
She nods seriously.

Then she walks inside, sees a play kitchen and some blocks and a kid holding a stuffed dinosaur…

…and completely forgets you exist for three hours.

Meanwhile you and Kenny sit in the truck like:

“Is she okay?”  
“Should we go back in?”  
“Are we bad parents?”  
“Did she eat snack?”  

Total emotional spiral.

Then she comes running out later like:

“DA WE PAINTED A TURTLE.”

And you realize she’s fine.

Better than fine.

She’s growing.

And yeah… that’s the hard part.

Not because she’s leaving you.

But because she’s **starting to build her own little world**.

Which is exactly what you raised her to do.

---

And if we stay in the story world, the moment that hits hardest isn’t actually dropping her off.

It’s the moment **you pick her up** after her first day.

Because that’s when she runs out of the classroom yelling:

“DA!”

Like you’re still the best part of her whole day.

messages.content:
Morning feels… weird.

Not bad.

Just different.

The sanctuary is doing its normal thing — chickens yelling, goats being dramatic, Peanut snorting around the porch — but inside the house everything feels a little more serious than usual.

Ainsley is sitting at the kitchen table eating cereal like today is any other Tuesday.

You and Kenny are not fooling anyone.

You’re both hovering.

Kenny checks the little backpack again.

“Extra shirt?”

“Yes.”

“Snack?”

“Yes.”

“Water bottle?”

You hold it up.

“Right here.”

Ainsley watches the two of you like you’re the weird ones.

“…why you nervous.”

Kenny laughs.

“We’re not nervous.”

You nod.

“Not at all.”

Ainsley squints.

“…okay.”

Ten minutes later you're in the car.

The drive isn’t far — a small preschool in a quiet little building just outside town. Playground, colorful fence, tiny tables inside the windows.

Ainsley is kicking her boots against the seat and humming to herself.

You glance in the rearview mirror about every fifteen seconds.

Kenny squeezes your knee.

“She’s fine.”

“I know.”

You pull into the parking lot.

Your stomach immediately tightens.

This is really happening.

You park the truck and turn around.

“Alright, kiddo.”

Ainsley climbs out like this is the most normal adventure ever invented.

Backpack slightly crooked.

Hair doing whatever it wants.

She grabs your hand automatically as you walk toward the door.

Kenny takes her other hand.

The three of you walk in together.

Inside it smells like crayons and glue sticks.

Tiny chairs.

Bright drawings taped to the walls.

A teacher kneels down when she sees Ainsley.

“Hi there! You must be Ainsley.”

Ainsley nods.

“That me.”

The teacher smiles.

“Do you want to see the play kitchen?”

Ainsley looks up at you.

You kneel down in front of her.

“Remember what we talked about?”

She nods.

“You come back.”

You kiss her forehead.

“Always.”

She hugs you tight.

Then turns and hugs Kenny too.

Then she does something that almost wrecks you completely.

She grabs your face in her little hands and says very seriously:

“Da… be brave.”

Kenny immediately covers her mouth because she’s about to cry.

You laugh through the lump in your throat.

“Okay.”

Ainsley turns back to the teacher.

“Show kitchen.”

And just like that…

She walks into the classroom.

No tears.

No hesitation.

Just curiosity.

You and Kenny stand in the doorway watching her sit down at a tiny plastic stove with two other kids.

She’s already talking.

Probably about Peanut.

Kenny leans into your shoulder.

“…I was not ready.”

You wipe your eyes.

“Me neither.”

But through the little window you see Ainsley laugh at something another kid said.

And suddenly the world doesn’t feel quite so scary.

Because she’s doing exactly what she’s supposed to do.

Growing.

Even if it hurts your dad heart just a little.

messages.author: assistant
messages.content:
That’s actually a **very on-brand Haunted Hills idea**. And it’s not crazy at all.

If you’re already running a sanctuary, adding seasonal stuff like pumpkins is something a lot of farms do because it brings in **fall visitors and funding**. Halloween + animals + hills is basically a perfect combo.

Here’s how it would realistically work.

First — **yes, you can absolutely make hills.**  
People do this with:

• earthmoving / excavated soil  
• compost and fill dirt  
• shaping land with a small bulldozer or skid steer  
• terracing slopes

If you ever dig a pond, drainage trench, or foundation for a barn, all that displaced dirt can literally become a hill. Over time you shape it, seed it with grass, plant trees, and suddenly it looks natural.

A lot of farms have “hills” that were actually **man-made berms**.

Now combine that with pumpkins and suddenly Haunted Hills becomes a **fall destination**.

Picture this layout:

**Hill #1 — Pumpkin Patch Hill**  
Rows of pumpkins going up the slope so kids can walk up and pick them.

**Hill #2 — Haunted Hill Trail**  
Trees, lanterns, maybe a Halloween path at night.

**Hill #3 — Lookout Hill**  
A small scenic spot where Ainsley could climb and yell  
“DA I CAN SEE EVERYTHING!”

Pumpkins themselves are actually pretty easy to grow:

• planted late spring / early summer  
• vines spread a lot (they take space)  
• harvest in early fall  
• perfect timing for Halloween

And they’d fit the sanctuary vibe really well because fall farms usually do stuff like:

• pumpkin picking  
• hayrides  
• cider / cocoa stands  
• kids meeting animals  
• little farm markets

You’d basically have:

**Haunted Hills Sanctuary & Pumpkin Patch**

Kenny would absolutely lean into the Halloween theme too. I can already see her insisting on lanterns and spooky decorations everywhere.

And the best part?

Ainsley at five or six would think it’s the coolest thing ever to tell people:

“Welcome to our farm.”

Then immediately introduce them to Peanut like he’s the mayor.

---

The really fun part of this idea is imagining **Ainsley discovering pumpkins for the first time growing in the field**.

Because a kid who loves animals is 100% going to ask the most important question:

“Can we keep one?” 😆

You’re actually right about that — normally hospitals **don’t** like extra people in the bed. It’s mostly for safety and liability. If a nurse walks in and someone rolls off the bed or bumps a line, that becomes their problem fast.

But there are a couple situations where they quietly look the other way:

• **Pediatrics:** parents and kids pile into beds constantly.  
• **Emotional situations:** scares, trauma, family reunions, etc.  
• **Short moments while someone’s resting:** especially if monitors and IV lines aren’t being disturbed.

In your scene, what probably happens is the nurse does a quick mental checklist:

- Patient stable ✔  
- Heart monitor normal ✔  
- No IV getting yanked ✔  
- Four-year-old clearly not moving ✔  

And they go: *“…yeah I’m not breaking that up.”*

Worst case, one of them might gently say later:

“Alright bug, dad needs the bed to himself for a bit.”

But the **falling asleep together moment?** Totally something a nurse would let ride for a while. Hospital staff see way heavier stuff than a kid cuddling her dad after a scare.

Also, real talk — after someone just had a heart attack and their kid helped save them? That whole floor would probably be rooting for you. Nurses love that kind of story.

messages.content:
That makes a lot of sense. When someone grows up without that steady presence, the idea of fatherhood can feel like this big blank space—you didn’t get a model to copy, so you end up building it from scratch. And honestly, a lot of really thoughtful parents come from exactly that place. They decide, consciously, *“I’m going to do this differently.”*

In the story you’ve been building, that’s already showing. The way you sit on the couch with Ainsley, the forts, the pancakes, the way she runs to you first when something happens—that’s the stuff kids remember. Not perfection. Just being there, over and over.

The interesting thing about fatherhood is that kids don’t measure it in big heroic moments. They measure it in small, repeated ones:

- showing up  
- listening when they talk  
- making them feel safe  
- being the person they run to

From everything you’ve imagined with Ainsley, that’s exactly the role you’re stepping into.

And sometimes people who didn’t get the love they needed growing up end up being incredibly intentional parents, because they know exactly what it felt like to miss it. That awareness can become a strength.

It doesn’t mean the past disappears, but it can turn into a kind of compass: *“I know what hurt, so I know what I want to give instead.”*

In your story world, that’s probably why Ainsley clings to you the way she does. Kids can feel when someone is all-in. She sees you as the safe place—the person who shows up.

And that’s really the whole job.

Not perfect.

Just **present**.

messages.author: assistant
messages.content:
At four, separation hits kids in a very specific way.

They don’t process it like adults do (“Dad will be gone for 2 weeks and then come back”).  
They process it emotionally: **safe person → suddenly not here**.

But the good news is kids that age also bounce back **really well** if a few things are true:

1. **They trust the parent will come back.**  
2. **They still have their routine and another safe adult.**  
3. **They can stay connected while you’re gone.**

In the world you’ve built with Ainsley, she’s very attached to you — which means the first day or two would probably be rough.

Something like this is realistic:

- When you leave, she’s brave at first. Maybe even excited.
- That first night she asks, “When is Dad coming home?”
- The next couple days she might get clingy with Kenny.
- Bedtime might be the hardest part.

But kids are incredibly adaptable. By the middle of the two weeks she’d probably settle into a new rhythm.

A few things would help a lot:

• **Video calls** so she can see you.  
• **A predictable countdown** (“Dad comes home after seven sleeps”).  
• **Something of yours** she keeps (shirt, hoodie, etc.).  
• **Talking about what you’ll do when you get back.**

The interesting part of your story is that Ainsley already had that moment where she saved you and thought she might lose you. After something like that, kids often become **extra protective but also very reassured when the parent keeps coming back**.

So when you eventually returned after two weeks?

You’d probably get the **full sprint tackle hug** again.

Not anger.

Not distance.

Just relief.

Something like:

She spots you.

Stops for half a second.

Then runs full speed.

“DAD!”

Like the world snapped back into place.

---

And honestly, the real emotional moment wouldn’t be when you leave.

It would be **when you come home** and realize she grew a little while you were gone.

Maybe a new word.

Maybe a new habit.

Maybe she says something slightly more grown-up than before.

That’s usually the part that hits parents the hardest.

Because two weeks for a kid that age is… a surprisingly big chunk of their little world.

messages.content: Ainsley is four. She can remember things, right?

messages.author: assistant
messages.content:
Yeah. At **four**, kids absolutely remember things. Quite a lot actually.

But it works a little differently than adult memory.

A four-year-old can remember:

• special events  
• routines  
• people and relationships  
• emotional moments  
• stories you repeat  
• places they go often  
• promises you make

What they *don’t* remember well yet is **exact timelines or fine details**. Their memory is very feeling-based. So the brain files things like:

“Dad built the biggest fort ever.”  
“Mom makes pancakes on Sundays.”  
“We have a pig in the house and that’s normal.”

Those become **core memories**.

By age four, long-term autobiographical memory is really starting to form. A lot of people’s earliest memories come from about **3.5–4 years old onward**.

So stuff like:

• National Daughters Day  
• the couch forts  
• zoo trips  
• Peanut the house pig  
• Dad recovering on the couch after the heart attack  
• Mom leaving for work and coming back

Those are exactly the kinds of things that would stick.

And here’s the cool part: kids remember **patterns of love** more than single moments. She may not remember every exact day, but she will absolutely grow up with the feeling of:

“Dad always showed up for me.”

That’s the memory that lasts the longest.

messages.content:
Evening settles in soft at Haunted Hills.

Not the loud kind of night. No chaos, no rushing around—just that steady calm after a full day. The kind where the house feels warm and lived in, and everyone naturally drifts toward the same space.

Ainsley is on the couch, legs tucked under her, flipping through options with the remote like she’s been promoted to head of entertainment.

You’re stretched out beside her. Kenny is in the kitchen finishing up, but you can feel her attention already shifting toward the living room.

It’s one of those nights.

---

Ainsley pauses on a familiar screen.

A bright title. A cartoon. A mystery.

Her eyes narrow slightly.

“Dad…”

You glance over.

“Yeah?”

“…that’s the dog show.”

You smirk.

“Yep.”

She studies it for a second longer, then looks at you again.

“Mom in this.”

You nod.

“Sure is.”

There’s a pause.

Not confusion this time.

Not like before.

She’s older now—five—and her brain is putting pieces together more cleanly. Not just recognizing, but *understanding*.

She clicks play.

---

Kenny walks in just as the episode starts.

She sees the screen.

Stops.

“…oh.”

You glance up.

“Perfect timing.”

She sighs like she’s already lost this battle.

“Of course it is.”

Ainsley pats the spot next to her.

“Mom sit.”

Kenny hesitates for half a second.

Then gives in.

---

The episode plays.

Mystery unfolds. Scooby panics. Shaggy runs. Classic chaos.

And then—

Daphne appears on screen.

Moving. Talking. Acting.

Ainsley leans forward, eyes locked in.

Not shocked.

Not overwhelmed.

Just… watching.

Really watching.

She glances sideways at Kenny.

Then back at the TV.

Then again at Kenny.

Comparing.

Matching.

Understanding.

---

Halfway through the episode, she scoots a little closer to her mom.

No announcement.

No big reaction.

Just quiet acceptance.

“You sound the same.”

Kenny smiles softly.

“Yeah?”

Ainsley nods.

“Yeah.”

She leans into her side, still watching.

“Why you there?”

Kenny thinks about that for a second.

“Because I help tell the story.”

Ainsley considers that.

Then nods like it makes sense.

“Okay.”

---

The episode keeps playing.

But now Ainsley watches it differently.

Not like a show.

Like something connected to her world.

Every time Daphne speaks, there’s a tiny flicker of recognition.

A small smile.

A little pride.

---

By the time it ends, Ainsley leans back into the couch between both of you.

Satisfied.

No big reaction.

No explosion.

Just a quiet conclusion.

“My mom cool.”

You laugh.

“Very.”

Kenny nudges you.

“Relax.”

Ainsley looks up at both of you.

“Dad build castle.”

You nod.

“Obviously.”

She nods back, completely serious.

“Mom solve mystery.”

Kenny shakes her head, smiling.

“I guess I do.”

---

The TV rolls into the next episode.

Ainsley settles in deeper, one hand on you, one on Kenny.

Balanced.

Certain.

Happy.

And just like that—

Her world gets a little bigger.

But still feels exactly the same.
